notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The two-stroke sign read e — tick, then body. Write it once.
こ (ko).
The simplest sign you have met. Two short horizontal strokes, stacked, the lower one longer and slightly curved:
the upper stroke, short, curving down a little at its right end.
the lower stroke, wider, sweeping right and lifting slightly.
Read ko: a clean k, then the o of English more shortened.
Nothing joins them. The gap between the two strokes is part of the shape — close it and you have a different sign.

segments.instruction: こ (ko) — upper stroke, then the longer lower one, and leave the gap
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: こ — upper stroke, then the longer lower one, and leave the gap]

segments.text: Say??? and tap all three morae before writing the new sign.
Which of the two strokes is longer? (The lower one.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke order per Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).

segments.prompt: How many strokes does the hiragana sign read 'ko' have?

feedback.incorrect: Two: a short upper stroke and a longer lower one.

segments.text: Two stacked strokes with a gap. Write the sign read ko.

blocks.title: Script — the shape, and the exception

segments.text: ん (n).
One stroke. Start with a small tick down-left, then sweep down, round to the right and up in a single unbroken movement, finishing with a rise.

Now the part that matters more than the shape. Every sign you have met so far is a consonant plus a vowel, or a vowel alone. This one is a consonant with no vowel at all — and it still takes a full beat, exactly as long as any other sign.

That is why Japanese counts morae rather than syllables, and it is the clearest evidence you will get. An English speaker hears the n at the end of a word as a tail on the vowel before it. Japanese does not. It is its own beat, held its own length, and shortening it is one of the most audible foreign-accent tells there is.

segments.instruction: ん — one continuous stroke, no lifts
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: ん — one continuous stroke, no lifts]

segments.instruction: hold it for a full beat, as long as any other sign takes
segments.source: [YOU SAY: hold it for a full beat, as long as any other sign takes]

segments.text: Cover the model and write?? from its two known signs.
If this sign has no vowel, how long is it held? (A full beat — the same as every other sign.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke order per Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).

segments.prompt: Which vowel does this sign carry?

feedback.correct: None — and it still takes a full beat.
feedback.incorrect: None at all. It is a consonant on its own, holding a whole beat.

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Write the three-stroke sign read ha. Vertical, crossbar, loop.
に (ni).
Three strokes, and the first one you have already practised:
the vertical down the left, with the same small flick left at the foot as the sign read ha.
a short horizontal to its right, upper area.
a longer horizontal below it, sweeping right.
Read ni: the n of knee, then the tight i you learned first.

This is the first time two signs share a visible part, and it is worth naming, because it is nearly the last. Hiragana is not built from recombining components the way Chinese characters are — these two happen to have worn down to similar left-hand posts, not because they mean or sound anything alike. Treat the resemblance as a handwriting convenience, not as a clue. Reading information into it is the mistake this book keeps warning you off.

segments.instruction: に (ni) — vertical, short bar, long bar
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: に — vertical, short bar, long bar]

segments.instruction: write it beside は and compare only the left post
segments.source: [YOU NOTICE: write it beside は and compare only the left post]

segments.text: Before the new sign, write? once and then? once from memory.
Which stroke of this sign comes first? (The vertical.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke order per Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).

segments.prompt: Two signs so far share a similar left-hand vertical. Does that shared shape tell you anything about their sound or meaning?

feedback.correct: Nothing — it is a handwriting resemblance, not a component.
feedback.incorrect: No. Hiragana signs are not built from meaningful parts; the resemblance is coincidental.

lessons.title: ち (chi) — two strokes, four roman letters, one beat
lessons.gloss: the hiragana sign for the mora chi — two strokes, and a sound the romanization spells with four letters

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Three strokes: vertical, short bar, long bar. Write the sign read ni.
ち (chi).
Two strokes:
a short horizontal across the top.
the body — down from the middle of that bar, curving left, then round into a full belly to the right and up.
Read chi: the ch of English cheese, then the tight i.

Count what just happened. One sign. One beat. Four roman letters to describe it. The romanization is a pronunciation aid written for people who do not read the script yet — it is not a smaller version of the writing system, and the number of letters in it tells you nothing about the number of beats in the word.
This is the moment the roman spelling starts costing you more than it pays, and it is why the signs are worth the effort.

segments.instruction: ち (chi) — top bar, then the body in one movement
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: ち — top bar, then the body in one movement]

segments.instruction: chi, one beat — as long as any other sign, no longer
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **chi**, one beat — as long as any other sign, no longer]

segments.text: Does the number of roman letters tell you how long a sign is held? (No.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke order per Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).

segments.prompt: This sign is romanised with four letters. How many beats does it take?

feedback.correct: One — the letter count is a description, not a measure.
feedback.incorrect: One beat. The four roman letters describe the sound; they do not count time.

lessons.title: わ — the sign for wa, and the trap beside it
lessons.gloss: the hiragana sign for the mora wa — and the sign the greeting does NOT end with, though it sounds like it

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Write the three-stroke sign read ha: vertical, crossbar, loop.
わ (wa).
Two strokes:
the vertical on the left, with the small flick at the foot.
the body — a short bar right from the top, then down, round to the left in a loop, and out to the lower right with a curl.
Read wa: like English wa in wander, one beat.

blocks.title: What you've built — and the trap

segments.text: Here is the thing this sign exists in this lesson to protect you from.
The daytime greeting sounds like it ends in wa. It is not written with this sign. It ends with the sign read ha — the one you learned early and were told was holding a second job.

That second job is grammatical: は is also Japanese's topic marker, and as a topic marker it is pronounced wa. The greeting is a frozen fragment of a longer sentence, and it kept the marker's spelling along with the marker's sound.
So the rule you need is not about sound at all:
わ is the sign for the mora wa inside ordinary words.
は read as wa means you are looking at the topic marker, or at something that used to contain one.

Getting this backwards is the single most common beginner spelling error in Japanese, and it is the reason this book taught you the sign for wa after you already knew the greeting — so the shape could arrive with its warning attached rather than be quietly assumed.

segments.instruction: わ (wa), then は beside it — two signs, one shared sound, different jobs
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: わ, then は beside it — two signs, one shared sound, different jobs]

segments.instruction: hearing wa at the end of the daytime greeting, which sign do you write?
segments.source: [YOU DECIDE: hearing *wa* at the end of the daytime greeting, which sign do you write?]

segments.text: Say??? again, keeping the two opening morae distinct.
Which of the two is a fact about grammar rather than about sound? (The one where は is read wa.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke order per Hitsujun Shido no Tebiki (Japanese Ministry of Education, 1958).

segments.prompt: The daytime greeting ends in a sound like 'wa'. Is it written with the sign for wa, or the sign for ha?

feedback.correct: The ha sign — it is the topic marker, and the marker is read wa.
feedback.incorrect: The HA sign. It is the topic marker, which is pronounced wa.

lessons.title: Five signs in a row — and the greeting is readable
lessons.gloss: five signs, all of them already yours — the greeting read rather than recalled

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the assembly and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Four signs, one after another, from memory. Say each beat as you finish writing it:
こ (ko) ん (n) に (ni) ち (chi).
Add the fifth — the one that is read wa because it is a topic marker — and the greeting is on the page:
こ + ん + に + ち + は becomes こんにちは (konnichiwa).
ko-n-ni-chi-wa. Five signs, five beats, all even. Say it against a steady tap and you will hear that the second beat, the one with no vowel, takes exactly as long as the four around it.

No new stroke appears here. You have decoded five pieces you can each write from memory, in order, including the one that sounds like something other than its name. The next lesson attaches the daytime-greeting meaning to the line.

Eight signs, taught one at a time, and with them you can now decode three whole sequences off the page. Two already carry useful answers; the five-sign sequence gets its daytime-greeting job in the next lesson.

Hiragana has forty-six basic signs. You hold eight. The rest arrive the same way, one per lesson, and the words they unlock arrive free — because a word in this script is never more than the signs you already own, in a row.

segments.instruction: こんにちは (konnichiwa) — sound each sign in turn; do not recall it whole
segments.source: [YOU READ: **こんにちは** — sound each sign in turn; do not recall it whole]

segments.instruction: the greeting, then say it once at speaking pace
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: the greeting, then say it once at speaking pace]

segments.text: Write? once, then set it beside? and name which one closes the greeting.
How many of the greeting's five signs were new in this lesson? (None.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart.

segments.prompt: How many beats (morae) does the written daytime greeting take?

feedback.correct: Five — one per sign, and the vowel-less one counts fully.
feedback.incorrect: Five: one beat per sign, including the one with no vowel.

lessons.title: こんにちは (konnichiwa) — hello, and a sign that lies about its sound

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — five familiar signs until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Retrieve はい and the sign は. You are about to meet は again in the daytime greeting — where it is not pronounced ha.
こんにちは (konnichiwa) — こ ko + ん n + に ni + ち chi + は.

You have written every sign separately. こ, に, and ち each carry a consonant and vowel. ん is the exception: a bare consonant with a full beat of its own. Read five signs in five beats: ko-n-ni-chi-wa. Do not swallow ん.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens — the sign は, read wa

segments.text: The last sign is は, which you learned as ha. Here it is read wa.
Here は is the topic particle, roughly "as for ___." It keeps an older spelling. Carry one small rule forward: read は as ha inside a word and as wa when it is the particle.
こんにちは (konnichiwa) is the daytime greeting. It began as an unfinished sentence: konnichi wa…, "as for today …" The rest fell away and the topic marker stayed.
The older phrase is often written with two kanji for "this day." You do not need to decode those yet. This chapter keeps the whole greeting in the hiragana signs you have already learned.

segments.instruction: こんにちは (konnichiwa) — ko-n-ni-chi-wa, five beats
は in はい becomes ha; は ending the greeting becomes wa
segments.source: [YOU DECIDE: **は** in **はい** → *ha*; **は** ending the greeting → *wa*]

segments.instruction: someone at midday becomes こんにちは (konnichiwa)
segments.source: [YOU GREET: someone at midday → **こんにちは**]

segments.text: Write? from memory and give it one full mora.
Which sign takes a beat without a vowel? (ん.) Why does the greeting end in a particle? (It is the opening of a sentence nobody finishes any more.)
Source: Wiktionary: こんにちは (konnichiwa).

segments.prompt: The greeting ends in the sign は. How is it pronounced there?

feedback.correct: Right: は is read wa when it works as the topic particle.
feedback.incorrect: It is read wa — は is the topic particle here, not the sound ha.
